steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting Tortoise, an authenticated encryption scheme built on a tweakable variant of AES. Motivate the need for trust and authenticated encryption, introduce the scheme and its properties, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Trust on the open Internet and the role of cryptography
- Authenticated encryption and why it matters
- Tortoise: an AEAD scheme built on a tweakable AES
- Properties and design choices of Tortoise
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Trust and cryptography
  - Internet = open platform for interaction; bad actors exploit unsuspecting users -> trust issues
  - cryptography-based systems as tool for trust
  - two categories: Symmetric-Key and Asymmetric-Key encryption (cite)
  - symmetric: same key for encryption/decryption; asymmetric: key pair (private, public)
- Authenticated encryption (AE)
  - parties exchange messages with secrecy and integrity
  - verify real identity of creator, prevent forgeries
  - present-day electronic transactions partly possible because of secure AE
  - our scheme uses Symmetric-Key primitive; unlike digital signatures (cite), asymmetric
- Tortoise
  - CAESER competitions (cite) show need for AE
  - Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) on well-known, well-studied cipher primitives
  - novel algorithm, tweakable variant of AES (cite)
  - generalizable framework: any block cipher (slightly modified for block sizes) -> AE scheme
- Properties
  - symmetric; parties encrypt and authenticate messages
  - AEAD: confidentiality, integrity, authentication
  - 128-bit message blocks; tweakable block size fixed by underlying cipher, AES (cite)
  - easy in hardware and software
  - nonce-resistant variant: full misuse-resistant AE (MRAE) security
  - long-term deployment on unmaintained edge devices -> prefer ciphers with long rigorous security review
- Organization
  - real-life demonstration of Tortoise
  - literature review Section 3, implementation Section 4, security analysis Section 5, limitations/future work/conclusions Sections 6 and 7

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The Internet is an open platform where users interact in many different ways. Because the web is open, there are trust issues, since bad actors take advantage of users who do not suspect anything. Systems based on cryptography can be the right tool to achieve trust. Cryptosystems fall into two broad categories, Symmetric-Key encryption and Asymmetric-Key encryption. In Symmetric-Key encryption the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt messages, and in Asymmetric-Key encryption a pair of keys (a private and a public key) is used for encryption and decryption.

Authenticated encryption (AE) lets multiple parties exchange messages with secrecy and integrity. Users can check the real identity of whoever created the message and prevent forged messages that would erode trust. Electronic transactions as we have them today are possible partly because secure authenticated encryption schemes were invented. In our work we use the Symmetric-Key encryption primitive to build our authenticated encryption scheme, which is different from digital signatures that focus on Asymmetric-Key encryption.

The recent CAESER competitions have shown that authenticated encryption schemes are needed. Our work introduces an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) scheme that is based on well-known cipher primitives whose security characteristics are well studied. Tortoise is a new cryptographic algorithm and it is based on a tweakable variant of AES. The scheme we propose gives a generalizable framework that can turn any block cipher (slightly modified so it accommodates different block sizes) into an authenticated encryption scheme.

- Properties
  - symmetric; parties encrypt and authenticate messages
  - AEAD: confidentiality, integrity, authentication
  - 128-bit message blocks; tweakable block size fixed by underlying cipher, AES
  - easy in hardware and software
  - nonce-resistant variant: full misuse-resistant AE (MRAE) security
  - long-term deployment on unmaintained edge devices -> prefer ciphers with long rigorous security review
- Organization
  - real-life demonstration of Tortoise
  - literature review Section 3, implementation Section 4, security analysis Section 5, limitations/future work/conclusions Sections 6 and 7

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The Internet is an open platform where users interact in many different ways. Because the web is open, there are trust issues, since bad actors take advantage of users who do not suspect anything. Systems based on cryptography can be the right tool to achieve trust. Cryptosystems fall into two broad categories, Symmetric-Key encryption and Asymmetric-Key encryption. In Symmetric-Key encryption the same key is used to encrypt and decrypt messages, and in Asymmetric-Key encryption a pair of keys (a private and a public key) is used for encryption and decryption.

Authenticated encryption (AE) lets multiple parties exchange messages with secrecy and integrity. Users can check the real identity of whoever created the message and prevent forged messages that would erode trust. Electronic transactions as we have them today are possible partly because secure authenticated encryption schemes were invented. In our work we use the Symmetric-Key encryption primitive to build our authenticated encryption scheme, which is different from digital signatures that focus on Asymmetric-Key encryption.

The recent CAESER competitions have shown that authenticated encryption schemes are needed. Our work introduces an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) scheme that is based on well-known cipher primitives whose security characteristics are well studied. Tortoise is a new cryptographic algorithm and it is based on a tweakable variant of AES. The scheme we propose gives a generalizable framework that can turn any block cipher (slightly modified so it accommodates different block sizes) into an authenticated encryption scheme.

Tortoise is a symmetric cryptographic scheme which lets parties communicate by encrypting and authenticating their messages. AEAD gives confidentiality, integrity and authentication. Tortoise uses 128 bits for message blocks. This tweakable cipher block size is however fixed in advance by the message block size of the underlying cipher, which is AES in our case. The algorithm is easy to implement both in hardware and in software. The nonce-resistant variant of Tortoise gives full misuse-resistant authenticated encryption (MRAE) security. Also, our design choices follow the expectation that the cipher is deployed for a long time on edge devices that are not maintained after they are installed. In this situation it is an advantage to deploy ciphers that have been through rigorous security review over a long period.

This paper presents a real-life demonstration of the Tortoise cipher. The paper is organized like this: a literature review in Section 3, an overview of the implementation in Section 4, and the security analysis in Section 5. At the end we give limitations, future work and conclusions in Section 6 and Section 7.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The Internet provides an open platform for many forms of interaction between users. Given the open nature of the web, there are trust issues due to bad actors taking advantage of unsuspecting users. Cryptography-based systems can provide the right tool for achieving trust. There are two broad categories of cryptosystems: Symmetric-Key encryption and Asymmetric-Key encryption [1]. Symmetric-Key encryption uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt messages, while Asymmetric-Key encryption uses a pair of keys (a private and a public key) for encryption and decryption.

Authenticated encryption (AE) allows multiple parties to exchange messages with secrecy and integrity. Users can verify the real identity of the message creator and prevent message forgeries that would erode trust. Present-day electronic transactions are possible partly due to the invention of secure authenticated encryption schemes. Our work uses the Symmetric-Key encryption primitive to build our authenticated encryption scheme, which is different from digital signatures [1] that focus on Asymmetric-Key encryption.

Recent CAESER competitions [2] have shown the need for authenticated encryption schemes. Our work introduces an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) scheme based on well-known cipher primitives with well-studied security characteristics. Tortoise is a novel cryptographic algorithm based on a tweakable variant of AES [3]. Our proposed scheme provides a generalizable framework capable of converting any block cipher (slightly modified to accommodate different block sizes) into an authenticated encryption scheme.

Tortoise is a symmetric cryptographic scheme that allows parties to communicate by encrypting and authenticating their messages. AEAD provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication. Tortoise uses 128 bits for message blocks; however, this tweakable cipher block size is predetermined by the message block size of the underlying cipher, which in our case is AES [3]. The algorithm is easy to implement in both hardware and software. The nonce-resistant variant of Tortoise provides full misuse-resistant authenticated encryption (MRAE) security. Furthermore, our design choices follow the expectation of long-term cipher deployment on edge devices that remain unmaintained after installation. In this situation, ciphers that have been subject to rigorous security review over an extended period are advantageous for deployment.

This paper presents a real-life demonstration of our Tortoise cipher and is organized as follows. We review the literature in Section 3, give an overview of our implementation in Section 4, and present the security analysis in Section 5. Finally, we provide limitations, future work, and conclusions in Section 6 and Section 7.

References:
[1] Diffie and Hellman (2006) Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman. 2006. New Directions in Cryptography. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22, 6 (2006), 644–654.
[2] cae (2001) 2001. CAESAR: Competition for Authenticated Encryption: Security, Applicability, and Robustness. https://competitions.cr.yp.to/caesar.html . Date accessed: September 26, 2023.
[3] aes (2001) 2001. Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/FIPS/NIST.FIPS.197-upd1.pdf . Date accessed: July 28, 2023.
